content:
A list circulating on social media, titled "Before you convert to Islam", tells a would-be convert to accept a set of "roles" first. One group of them concerns people who have left Islam.

The convert must "criminalize apostate", "witch hunt apostate", support the "death penalty for apostate", "deny ex Muslim people existence", "discriminate apostate" and avoid them "for all cost". Another concerns sexuality: "Reject your LGBT friends because they are abomination", and if the convert is LGBT, "go to conversion therapy reject your identity, start hating yourself".

The list presents these as duties every convert takes on. This article aims to provide context to those two groups of claims, insha'Allah, in seven answers: what a convert actually owes to people who leave Islam, what the classical law and modern scholars said about apostasy, and what the sources say about same-sex desire, acts and friendship. Two companion articles take up what a convert actually takes on and the list's claims about women.

The Quran frames both questions with the principle a convert accepts on the day he enters: "There shall be no compulsion in [acceptance of] the religion" (2:256).[1]

The list tells the convert to "deny ex Muslim people existence". The Quran does the opposite: it names them.

"How shall Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their belief" (3:86). "Indeed, those who have believed then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, and then increased in disbelief" (4:137).[1]

It even records a tactic of leaving: some of the People of the Scripture told each other to "believe in that which was revealed to the believers at the beginning of the day and reject it at its end that perhaps they will abandon their religion" (3:72).[1] A scripture that describes apostasy in these terms does not ask its followers to pretend that apostates do not exist.

The Quran also separates outward words from inner belief. A person "forced [to renounce his religion] while his heart is secure in faith" is excused (16:106).[1] The judgement on belief belongs to God. The Quran places the consequence of leaving in the next life: "whoever of you reverts from his religion [to disbelief] and dies while he is a disbeliever - for those, their deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter" (2:217).[1] The verse speaks of a reckoning with God, and it gives the believer no task of pursuit. The other verses on leaving the faith (3:86–90; 4:137) also speak of God's judgement, and none of them names a worldly penalty.[1]

The list's "witch hunt" has no place in the sources. The Quran commands: "avoid much [negative] assumption. Indeed, some assumption is sin. And do not spy" (49:12).[1] The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "do not look for the others' faults and do not spy, and do not be jealous of one another, and do not desert (cut your relation with) one another".[2]

When Usāma ibn Zayd killed a man in battle after the man had said "There is no god but Allah", claiming he had said it only from fear, the Prophet asked him: "Did you tear his heart in order to find out whether it had professed or not?" He kept repeating it until Usāma wished he had only entered Islam that day.[3] The sources forbid the very inquiry into hearts that a witch hunt needs.

The list asks the convert to support the "death penalty for apostate". We state the classical record as it is.

Al-Bukhārī records the report: "Whoever changed his Islamic religion, then kill him".[4] Ibn Ḥajar sets it out under the heading of the ruling on the apostate man and woman and asking them to repent.[5]

Modern scholars have read it differently. In 2007 the Grand Mufti of Egypt, ʿAlī Jumʿa, wrote: "can a person who is Muslim choose a religion other than Islam? The answer is yes, they can", and called it a matter between the individual and God.[6]

At Ḥudaybiya, the Prophet accepted a treaty term under which any Muslim who left for Mecca would not be returned. He said of such a person: "One who goes away from us to join them, may Allah keep him away".[7]

He did not send anyone after them. We set out the full debate in our article on apostasy in Islam.

The list tells the convert to "discriminate apostate" and to "disassociate" from them for peace of mind. The Quran's rule for dealing with people who do not share one's faith is justice and good conduct: "Allah does not forbid you from those who do not fight you because of religion and do not expel you from your homes - from being righteous toward them and acting justly toward them" (60:8).[1]

The Quran applies the rule to the hardest case, parents who press their child to abandon the faith. "Do not obey them but accompany them in [this] world with appropriate kindness" (31:15).[1] If a convert must treat parents who oppose his faith with kindness, he cannot be required to discriminate against a friend or relative who has left it.

The Prophet applied the rule himself. When the mother of Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr, who was still a pagan, came to visit her daughter hoping for her generosity, Asmāʾ asked whether she should keep good relations with her. He answered: "Yes, keep good relation with her."[8] Family ties survive a difference of religion, in either direction.

We set out what former Muslims' accounts show, and what a Muslim reader owes the writer, in our article on what former Muslims' testimonies show.

The list says a convert must reject LGBT friends "because they are abomination". We state the Islamic position plainly.

The Quran condemns the people of Lot for their acts: "Indeed, you approach men with desire, instead of women. Rather, you are a transgressing people" (7:81).[1] Sexual acts between people of the same sex are forbidden in Islamic law.

The prohibition concerns acts. The Prophet said: "Allah has forgiven my followers the evil thoughts that occur to their minds, as long as such thoughts are not put into action or uttered."[9] A desire a person did not choose and does not act on is not counted against him, and "Allah does not charge a soul except [with that within] its capacity" (2:286).[1]

The list calls people "abomination". The sources forbid that kind of speech about anyone: "do not insult one another and do not call each other by [offensive] nicknames" (49:11).[1]

When a man was punished for drinking and someone cursed him, the Prophet said: "Do not curse him, for by Allah, I know for he loves Allah and His Apostle".[10] We set out the texts and the classical law in our article on homosexuality in Islam.

The list tells an LGBT convert to "go to conversion therapy", "reject your identity" and "start hating yourself". No verse of the Quran and no report of the Prophet prescribes any therapy for desire, and none commands self-hatred. The law addresses what a person does, and the Prophet's words on unacted thoughts set the limit.[9]

The Quran addresses every person with honour: "We have certainly honored the children of Adam" (17:70), and "We have certainly created man in the best of stature" (95:4).[1] To a person weighed down by sin, real or feared, it says: "do not despair of the mercy of Allah. Indeed, Allah forgives all sins" (39:53).[1]

A Muslim with same-sex desire is asked what every Muslim is asked about desire outside marriage: to keep from the act. The Prophet's advice to young people who could not marry was to fast, because it helps a person guard his modesty.[11] Hating oneself appears nowhere in that advice.

The list tells the convert to reject LGBT friends. A friend who is LGBT is first a person, and the convert's duty toward any person who does not fight him is righteousness and justice (60:8).[1] A Muslim does not endorse an act he believes is forbidden, and he is not asked to; he is also not asked to cut off people.

The Prophet's instruction is general: "do not desert (cut your relation with) one another, and do not hate one another".[2] A convert keeps his own conduct within the law and keeps his manners with everyone. That combination is harder than the list's instruction to reject, and it is what the sources ask.

The Prophet's own conduct shows the pattern. A young Jewish boy used to serve him, and when the boy fell sick the Prophet went to visit him and sat by his head.[12] He did not wait for the boy to share his faith before treating him as a person owed care, and a convert who follows him extends the same care to his friends.

The bottom line

The Quran names those who leave Islam and forbids spying on anyone's faith. The Prophet forbade searching hearts.

The classical law did prescribe a penalty for apostasy, after a call to repent, and modern scholars such as Egypt's Grand Mufti have said that a Muslim may change his religion as a matter between him and God. No source asks a convert to hunt, deny or discriminate against anyone who leaves.

On sexuality, Islam forbids same-sex acts and does not count unacted desire as a sin. It prescribes neither conversion therapy nor self-hatred, and it forbids cursing people.

A convert's duty toward LGBT friends, and toward friends who have left Islam, is the duty of 60:8: righteousness and justice. God knows best.

Notes

  1. Quran 2:256; 3:86; 4:137; 3:72; 16:106; 2:217; 49:12; 60:8; 31:15; 7:81; 2:286; 17:70; 95:4; 39:53; 49:11, Saheeh International translation.
  2. Sahih al-Bukhari 6064, report of Abū Hurayra.
  3. Sahih Muslim 96, report of Usāma ibn Zayd.
  4. Sahih al-Bukhari 6922, report of ʿIkrima from Ibn ʿAbbās.
  5. Ibn Ḥajar al-ʿAsqalānī, Fatḥ al-Bārī sharḥ Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī (Cairo: al-Maṭbaʿa al-Salafiyya), vol. 12, p. 267, on Sahih al-Bukhari 6922, the chapter on the ruling on the apostate and asking him to repent.
  6. Khadiga Samir, "Grand Mufti: Muslims may convert to other religions", Daily News Egypt, 24 July 2007, https://dailynewsegypt.com/2007/07/24/grand-mufti-muslims-may-convert-to-other-religions/, on ʿAlī Jumʿa's contribution to the Washington Post-Newsweek forum On Faith.
  7. Sahih Muslim 1784, report of Anas ibn Mālik on the treaty of al-Ḥudaybiya.
  8. Sahih al-Bukhari 2620, report of Asmāʾ bint Abī Bakr.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari 5269, report of Abū Hurayra.
  10. Sahih al-Bukhari 6780, report of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 5066, report of ʿAbd Allāh ibn Masʿūd.
  12. Sahih al-Bukhari 1356, report of Anas ibn Mālik.
